docs.title: What is crimepy?
docs.text: crimepy downloads, combines, munges, analyzes, and plots crime data. It starts with the FBI's National Incident-Based Reporting System (NIBRS): the yearly master files of every incident that participating law enforcement agencies reported, from 1991 to the latest year, published by the FBI's Crime Data Explorer. crimepy turns those fixed-width files into flat tables that work in pandas, and it is built on amos: every table is an amos.Dataset, every analysis is an amos technique, and a whole study (from loading the data to modeling and figures) can be described in a settings file.

docs.title: Why use crimepy?
docs.text:
• Any year, in one line. crimepy.nibrs.load('victims', '2015-2023') downloads the master files that are missing, parses them, and returns one table, with "data_year" saying which year each row came from.
  • Ready for amos. Tables come as amos datasets, which hold the data (a pandas data frame), its label and groups for modeling, and the tables, figures, and models that analyses add to them, so any amos model, validator, or plot works on them directly.
  • Flat tables with labels. Every segment of the master files becomes a table with one column per field. Codes become labeled categories ("20" becomes "Residence/Home"), dates become dates, ages become numbers, and missing values are missing (pd.NA), not blanks or zeros.
  • Fast and frugal. Each year is parsed once (a recent year, over 6 GB of text, takes about five minutes) and saved as compressed parquet files. After that, loading a table of a whole year takes seconds, and loading a few states or columns takes less.
  • Joined for analysis. crimepy.nibrs.tables joins an incident's segments into tables of incidents, victims, offenses, offenders, or arrestees, each with its incident's and agency's details: whether the incident was cleared, how many days until an arrest, the victim's relationship to the offender, the agency's population, and more.
  • Every year's quirks handled. The master files changed over three decades: batch headers split into three records before 2013, fields added in 2013, records padded to 132 characters or trimmed, and some years compressed with Deflate64, which Python's zipfile cannot read. crimepy reads them all and gives every year the same columns.
  • Analysis and figures included. Counts, trends, crime rates that use only agencies that reported all year, clearance rates, cross-tabulations, and reporting coverage, and figures of trends, the most common values, the hours and days of incidents, and age pyramids.
  • Reproducible studies. Every analysis and figure is an amos technique, so a study can load NIBRS data, reshape it, model it, and draw it from a plain settings file that doubles as a description of the methods.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: crimepy requires Python 3.11 or later and runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows. Recent master files are about 600 MB to download, and their converted tables are about 500 MB on disk. Downloads and tables are saved in the "crime" folder of the data folder of amos's workspace, the folder that holds your "code" folder (such as "projects/data/crime" for code in "projects/code"), where amos projects look for data too, unless you set the CRIMEPY_DATA environment variable or crimepy.options.DATA_FOLDER (or pass folder to any function).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
To install crimepy, use pip:

pip install crimepy

To also install every optional package that amos can use for analysis (such as statsmodels and the boosting models):

pip install crimepy[analysis]

docs.title: Load NIBRS data
docs.text:
import crimepy

victims = crimepy.nibrs.load('victims', years = '2021-2023', states = 'DE')
victims.data[['data_year', 'incident_date', 'offense_1', 'victim_age', 'victim_sex']].head()

load returns an amos.Dataset, whose data is the table (a pandas data frame). Pass label (and groups) to make it ready for modeling: crimepy.nibrs.load('victims', 2023, label = 'victim_age'). The first call downloads and converts each year, which takes a few minutes for a recent year. The tables of the master files are:

Table One row for each agencies agency: location, population, type, and the months it reported administrative incident: date, hour, numbers of segments, and exceptional clearance offenses offense of an incident: offense, location, weapons, and bias motivations properties property loss of an incident: type of loss, description, value, and drugs victims victim: offenses, age, sex, race, injuries, and relationships to offenders offenders offender: age, sex, race, and ethnicity arrestees arrestee of an incident: date and type of arrest, offense, and person group_b_arrests arrest for a Group "B" offense (such as disorderly conduct or DUI) window_clearances, window_properties, window_arrestees partial report of an incident that began before its agency reported to NIBRS

Pass columns to load only some columns, and decode = False to keep the FBI's codes instead of their labels. crimepy.nibrs.load_frame returns the table as a plain data frame. crimepy.nibrs.read reads tables straight from a master file, without saving anything, which suits a quick look:

datasets = crimepy.nibrs.read('nibrs-2023.zip', limit = 100_000)
datasets['offenses'].data.head()

docs.title: Combine the segments of incidents
docs.text:
incidents = crimepy.nibrs.tables.build('incidents', '2021-2023', states = 'DE')
incidents.data[['incident_date', 'offense_count', 'firearm', 'arrested', 'days_to_arrest', 'cleared']].head()

build makes a dataset with one row for each of the incidents, victims, offenses, offenders, or arrestees, with the details of its incident and agency. crimepy.combine.stack and crimepy.combine.merge stack and join any datasets (or data frames) while keeping their categories.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
from crimepy import analyze

agencies = crimepy.nibrs.load('agencies', '2021-2023', states = 'DE')
analyze.crime_rates(incidents, agencies, by = ['data_year', 'state'])
analyze.clearance_rates(incidents, by = ['data_year', 'agency_population_group'])
analyze.trend(incidents, date = 'incident_date', freq = 'MS')
analyze.coverage(agencies)

victims = crimepy.nibrs.tables.build('victims', 2023, states = 'DE')
analyze.crosstab(victims, 'victim_sex', 'relationship', normalize = 'index')

Each function applies an amos technique (see crimepy.techniques) and returns its table, which a dataset also keeps in its tables (such as incidents.tables['clearance_rates']). count makes a new dataset of counts, ready to model. crime_rates counts only agencies that reported in every month of the year, both for the crimes and for the population, so that agencies that did not report do not lower the rates. Without a table of agencies, it loads the agencies of the data's years and states.

docs.title: Plot
docs.text:
offenses = crimepy.nibrs.tables.build('offenses', '2021-2023', states = 'DE')
figure = crimepy.plot.trend(offenses, by = 'offense_category', top = 5, freq = 'QS')
figure.savefig('trend.png')
crimepy.plot.top_values(offenses, 'location')
crimepy.plot.time_heatmap(incidents)
crimepy.plot.age_pyramid(victims, person = 'victim')

Each function returns the figure, and a dataset also keeps it in its figures (such as offenses.figures['trend_plot']).

Figures have amos's style for scientific journals, with colors that people with color blindness can tell apart.

docs.title: Describe a study in a settings file
docs.text:
Every crimepy technique is an amos technique, so a study can be a settings file. This one loads three years of Delaware's incidents, counts them by size of agency, month, and day of the week, and compares two models of the counts (poisson needs pip install crimepy[analysis]):

[general]
seed = 43
label = count

[crime_project]
crime_workers = wrangler, analyst, critic

[wrangler]
techniques = load_nibrs, count_crimes

[load_nibrs_parameters]
table = incidents
years = 2021-2023
states = DE

[count_crimes_parameters]
by = agency_population_group, incident_month, incident_weekday

[analyst]
design = experiment
criterion = rmse
steps = split, encode, model
split_techniques = train_test
encode_techniques = one_hot
model_techniques = poisson, random_forest

[critic]
techniques = scorecard

project = crimepy.Project.create('crime.ini')
project.scorecard.table

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
crimepy nibrs years
crimepy nibrs download 2021-2023
crimepy nibrs convert 2021-2023
crimepy nibrs export victims 2023 --states DE MD --output victims.csv
crimepy project crime.ini --export

See the tutorial, the advanced user guide (which explains the master files and every choice crimepy makes in reading them), and the recipes.

docs.title: Advanced User Guide
docs.text: This guide explains the NIBRS master files and every choice that crimepy makes in reading them, so that you can describe your data accurately and check crimepy's work.

docs.title: The NIBRS master files
docs.text:
The FBI's Crime Data Explorer (CDE) publishes one master file of NIBRS data for each year from 1991. Each is a zip archive of one text file, from about 25 MB (1991) to about 600 MB (recent years) compressed, and over 6 GB of text for recent years. Every line is a record of one segment of a report, and the first two characters of a record are its segment level:

Level Segment crimepy table BH (B1, B2, B3 before 2013) Batch header: one agency agencies 01 Administrative: one incident administrative 02 Offense offenses 03 Property properties 04 Victim victims 05 Offender offenders 06 Arrestee arrestees 07 Group "B" Arrest Report group_b_arrests W1 Window exceptional clearance window_clearances W3 Window recovered property window_properties W6 Window arrestee window_arrestees

The records are sorted by state and agency. Each agency's batch header comes first, followed by its incidents, each of which is a "record set" of its administrative segment and then its other segments in order of level.

docs.title: Where the fields are
docs.text:
The positions of the fields come from the FBI's "NIBRS Flatfile Yearly Master Record Descriptions" (dated 12/18/95), which the CDE still distributes with the master files (crimepy.nibrs.cde.download_documentation downloads it). The document describes both fixed-length records (padded to 132 characters) and variable-length records (which end at their last field), and its positions are the same for both.

The FBI added fields to the files after 1995 that the document does not describe. crimepy found them by profiling every position of the files from 2004 to 2025 and includes them:

Segment Positions Field In the files crimepy column Administrative 89 Cargo theft (Y or N) 2013 and later cargo_theft Offense 60-67 Bias motivations #2 to #5 2013 to 2016 (later years drop them) bias_motivation_2 to bias_motivation_5 Victim 124-135 The type of activity and assignment of a law enforcement officer who was a victim, and the ORI of another jurisdiction (handwritten into the document) Every year officer_activity, officer_assignment, officer_other_ori Offender 40 Ethnicity of the offender 2013 and later offender_ethnicity Batch header 285-292 A date that is the same for every agency in a state, which the FBI does not document 2013 to 2016 state_nibrs_date

Fields that a year's records do not have are missing in that year.

docs.title: Batch headers
docs.text:
Before 2013, each agency's batch header was split into three records: B1 (the agency's location and type), B2 (the populations of its first four counties), and B3 (its fifth county, the months it reported, and its FIPS county codes). From 2013, one BH record has all of them. crimepy joins the three records into one row, so the agencies table has the same columns in every year.

The agencies table has, for each agency:

  • Its location: city, state, division, region, judicial_district, field_office, and, for each of up to five counties, ucr_county_1, msa_1, and fips_county_1 (and so on).
  • Its size and type: population_group, agency_type, core_city, and the current and previous census populations of each county (population_1 and last_population_1, and so on). population is the sum of the counties' populations.
  • Its reporting: date_ori_went_nibrs, nibrs_active, covered_by_ori (the agency that reports for it, if any), months_reported, and, for each month, whether it submitted a zero report (zero_report_jan), a Group "A" or "B" report (incident_report_jan), and a window record (window_report_jan). months_active is the number of months in which it submitted a zero report or a report of incidents.

docs.title: Linking the segments of an incident
docs.text:
The segments of an incident share the agency's ORI and the incident number, and crimepy adds data_year (the year of the master file), so ["data_year", "ori", "incident_number"] (crimepy.nibrs.tables.KEYS) identifies an incident. Incident numbers are encrypted by the FBI in most years, so they cannot be linked to other records. A few incidents appear more than once in a file (193 of the 12.4 million in 2023, each an exact duplicate), and crimepy.nibrs.tables.incidents keeps the first.

The FBI notes that the records after a batch header have the same first seven characters of the ORI as the header, but that the last two may differ. So crimepy adds agency_ori to every record: the ORI of the batch header that the record follows. Agencies are joined to incidents by agency_ori.

A Group "B" Arrest Report has no incident, and its positions 14-25 are the arrest transaction number (arrest_transaction_number), not an incident number.

docs.title: Compression
docs.text: The CDE compressed the master files for 2017 to 2023 that it published before August 2026 with Deflate64, a variant of Deflate that Python's zipfile cannot read. crimepy reads those files with inflate64, without extracting them. The files that the CDE publishes now use Deflate, but copies downloaded earlier still work.

docs.title: Kinds of fields
docs.text:
Each field of a layout (crimepy.nibrs.layouts) has a kind, which decides what it becomes:

Kind Becomes Example code a category (labeled if decode is true) location "20" becomes "Residence/Home" text text without blanks around it the ORI, incident number, or city int a whole number (Int64), missing if blank incident_hour, property_value date a date (datetime64), missing if blank or impossible incident_date ("20230101") bool true for "Y", false for "N", missing otherwise cargo_theft, core_city yes true if the field is a given character, false otherwise report_date ("R"), weapon_1_automatic ("A") quantity a number with thousandths drug_quantity_1 ("000000001250" becomes 1.25)

docs.title: Values with special meanings
docs.text:
• Ages. Age codes are kept (as victim_age_code, and so on), and crimepy adds the age in years (victim_age): "NN" (under 24 hours), "NB" (1 to 6 days), and "BB" (7 to 364 days) are 0, "99" (99 or older) is 99, and "00" (unknown) is missing.
  • Offender sequence 0. An offender whose sequence number is 0 is unknown (nothing is known about the offender). incidents counts only known offenders in offender_count.
  • Report dates. If report_date is true, the incident date is the date that the incident was reported, because the date that it happened is not known.
  • Incident hour. A blank hour is unknown (missing), and an incident at midnight is in hour 0.
  • Property values. The FBI asks agencies to report a value of $1 when the value is unknown, so a value of 1 usually means unknown. crimepy keeps the reported value.
  • Automatic weapons. weapon_1_automatic is false when there is no weapon.

docs.title: Labels
docs.text:
crimepy.nibrs.codes has the labels of every code, following the reference tables that the CDE publishes with its NIBRS downloads (such as NIBRS_OFFENSE_TYPE.csv) and, for fields that are only in the master files (such as the batch header's population group), the record descriptions. Codes changed over the years, and each codebook has every code that any year uses. A few codes meant something else in earlier years:

  • Race "A" was "Asian or Pacific Islander" before 2013, when "P" (Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander) was added.
  • Exceptional clearance "C" was "Extradition Denied" in the 1995 document and is "In Custody of Other Jurisdiction" now.

A code that is not in a codebook (such as agency type "5" in some early years) is kept as it is, so nothing is lost. To use your own labels, pass them to crimepy.nibrs.decode:

offenses = crimepy.nibrs.load('offenses', 2023, decode = False)
offenses = crimepy.nibrs.decode(
    offenses, ['location'], {'location': {'20': 'Home', '13': 'Street'}})

offenses, arrestees, and group_b_arrests also get the category of the offense (offense_category, such as "Assault Offenses"), whom or what it is against (crime_against: "Person", "Property", "Society", or "Not a Crime"), and its group (offense_group: "A" or "B"), from the CDE's table of offenses (with the prefix "arrest_" for arrests). crimepy.nibrs.codes.OFFENSE_TYPES lists the offense codes that are against each of them, and those of a few types that cut across the categories ("National Security Offenses", "Rape Offenses", "Sex Offenses", and "Immigration Offenses"), such as for picking the crimes against property:

property_crimes = crimepy.nibrs.codes.OFFENSE_TYPES['Property']

docs.title: Where the data are saved
docs.text:
Everything is saved in the data folder: the CRIMEPY_DATA environment variable, if it is set, and otherwise the "crime" folder (crimepy.options.DATA_SUBFOLDER) of the data folder of amos's workspace. The workspace is the folder that holds the "code" folder above the current folder (or the folder named by the AMOS_WORKSPACE environment variable; see amos's Clerk), so the data are kept outside every project, and an amos project's results are kept beside them, in the workspace's "studies" folder. Change the data folder for a session with crimepy.options.DATA_FOLDER, or pass folder to any function.

projects/                (amos's workspace)
    code/                (your projects' code)
    studies/             (the results of amos projects)
    data/
        crime/           (crimepy's data folder)
            nibrs/
                raw/
                    nibrs-2023.zip
                tables/
                    2023/
                        administrative.parquet
                        agencies.parquet
                        ...

The parquet files have the codes (not the labels) and are compressed with zstd, so a recent year takes about 500 MB. They can be read by any tool that reads parquet (such as R's arrow or DuckDB). Delete a year's folder in "tables" to convert it again, or pass overwrite = True to crimepy.nibrs.convert.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: crimepy parses a master file in chunks of a million records (crimepy.options.CHUNK_SIZE), so converting even the largest year needs little memory. A whole table of a recent year is large in memory, though: the 2023 administrative table has 12.4 million rows and takes about 1.6 GB. Pass states and columns to load to keep only what you need. They are applied while the parquet files are read, so the rest is never loaded.

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text:
crimepy is built on amos, so its tables are amos.Datasets:

  • crimepy.nibrs.load, load_tables, read, and tables.build return datasets, whose data is the table (a pandas data frame). They take label, task, and groups, which amos models, splitters, and validators use. crimepy.nibrs.load_frame returns a plain data frame.
  • Every function of crimepy.analyze, crimepy.combine, and crimepy.plot (and crimepy.nibrs.decode) takes a dataset or a data frame.
  • The analyses and figures are amos techniques. A describer's table is kept in the dataset's tables and a figure in its figures, under the technique's name, and every step is recorded in its history. count makes a new dataset of counts, whose label is the counts.
  • crimepy.combine.stack and merge return a dataset with the label and groups of the first dataset given, if their columns are still there.

A dataset gathers the data, what was learned from it, and how, so it is the record of an analysis. Any amos technique (a model, a validator, a metric, or a plot such as shap_beeswarm) can be applied to it directly, as in the tutorial.

docs.title: The amos techniques
docs.text:
Importing crimepy adds these techniques to the amos library:

Technique Kind What it does load_nibrs loader loads a table (or builds one) for years, with years, table, states, columns, decode, and folder parameters decode_nibrs munger replaces codes with labels count_crimes shaper counts rows by by (and periods of freq), so counts can be modeled crime_trend describer a table of counts over time population_rates describer counts per 100,000 people, from a table of counts crime_rates describer crimes per 100,000 people, using only agencies that reported all year (loading the agencies of the data's years and states) clearance_rates describer a table of clearance rates by group percent_change describer the change from one period to the next crosstab describer counts or shares of two columns against each other coverage describer the agencies that reported and the people they serve, from a table of agencies trend_plot, top_values, time_heatmap, age_pyramid plots the figures of crimepy.plot

The functions of crimepy.analyze and crimepy.plot apply them. Name them in any worker of an amos settings file, with parameters in a {technique}_parameters section. See the amos documentation for the rest of a project's settings.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

• Breaking: crimepy.nibrs.codes.STATES is now the name of each numeric state code (it was STATE_NAMES), and codes.STATE_ABBREVIATIONS is the postal abbreviation (it was STATES).
  • Each codebook of crimepy.nibrs.codes.CODEBOOKS is also public by itself (such as codes.RACES and codes.WEAPONS). The "clearances" codebook is codes.EXCEPTIONAL_CLEARANCES, and the "divisions" codebook is codes.SUBREGIONS. codes.OFFENSES has the name, category, whom or what it is against, and group of each offense code.
  • crimepy.nibrs.codes.OFFENSE_TYPES lists the offense codes of each type: whom or what they are against ("Person", "Property", "Society", and "Not a Crime"), and "National Security Offenses", "Rape Offenses", "Sex Offenses", and "Immigration Offenses".
  • The code follows the house style throughout: lines of at most 80 characters (the tables in docstrings are now lists), section markers that group the members of each module and class, and a full docstring for every function and method, tests and private ones included.

• Breaking: crimepy keeps its data in amos's workspace (amos 0.6.0), not in a "crimepy_data" folder of the home folder. The data folder is now the "crime" folder (options.DATA_SUBFOLDER) of the data folder of the workspace that holds the "code" folder (such as "projects/data/crime" for code in "projects/code"; see amos's Clerk), so NIBRS is in "data/crime/nibrs", beside the "studies" folder of amos projects' results. CRIMEPY_DATA, options.DATA_FOLDER (now None unless CRIMEPY_DATA is set), and a folder argument still name another. Move an existing "crimepy_data" folder's "nibrs" folder there (or set CRIMEPY_DATA) to keep its downloads and tables. Requires amos 0.6.0.

• Breaking: crimepy is built on amos datasets. crimepy.nibrs.load, load_tables, read, and tables.build (and its builders) return amos.Datasets, whose data is the table, and take label, task, and groups for modeling. crimepy.nibrs.load_frame returns a plain data frame, as load did. crimepy.combine.stack and merge return datasets, and crimepy.analyze.count returns a new dataset of counts, whose label is the counts.
  • Every analysis is an amos technique: population_rates, crime_rates, percent_change, crosstab, and coverage join count_crimes, crime_trend, and clearance_rates. The functions of crimepy.analyze apply them, take datasets or data frames, and keep their tables in a dataset's tables. crime_rates loads the agencies of the data's years and states when it is given none.
  • The functions of crimepy.plot take datasets, which keep their figures in figures, and crimepy.nibrs.decode decodes a dataset in place.
  • Downloads of master files that break (as they do when the CDE's 15-minute link expires during a slow download) resume where they stopped, with a new link.
  • crimepy requires amos 0.4.1.
  • The README has a BibTeX entry for citing crimepy, and CITATION.cff has the date of the release.

• Initial version, from the snickerdoodle template, built on amos.
  • crimepy.nibrs downloads the FBI's NIBRS master files for any year from 1991 (download), converts them to parquet files (convert), and loads their tables into pandas for any years, states, and columns (load). It reads every era of the files: the three batch header records before 2013, the fields added in 2013, fixed-length and variable-length records, and archives compressed with Deflate64.
  • crimepy.nibrs.layouts has the position of every field, from the FBI's record descriptions and from fields found in the files, and crimepy.nibrs.codes has the label of every code.
  • crimepy.nibrs.tables joins the segments of incidents into tables of incidents, victims, offenses, offenders, and arrestees, with the details of their incidents and agencies.
  • crimepy.combine stacks and joins tables while keeping their categories.
  • crimepy.analyze counts events, makes trends, crime rates, clearance rates, and cross-tabulations, and measures reporting coverage.
  • crimepy.plot draws trends, the most common values, events by hour and day, and age pyramids.
  • amos techniques: load_nibrs, decode_nibrs, count_crimes, crime_trend, clearance_rates, trend_plot, top_values, time_heatmap, and age_pyramid.
  • A command line interface: crimepy nibrs years, download, convert, and export, and crimepy project.

docs.title: Environment Setup
docs.text:
Install uv, then create a virtual environment with all of the development dependencies from the repository folder:

uv sync

Then, install the pre-commit hooks so that they run before each commit:

uv run pre-commit install

Run the tests with uv run pytest.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
Follow this basic process:

  1. Fork and clone the repository.
  2. Create a new branch: git checkout -b feature-or-bugfix-name.
  3. Edit the code.
  4. If you added functionality or features, update the documentation accordingly.

If you are unsure about how to fix or ignore a warning, just let the continuous integration fail, and we will help you during review.

Don't bother updating the changelog, we will take care of this.

docs.title: Pull requests guidelines
docs.text:
Link to any related issue in the Pull Request message.

During the review, we recommend using fixups:

# SHA is the SHA of the commit you want to fix
git commit --fixup=SHA

Once all the changes are approved, you can squash your commits:

git rebase -i --autosquash main

And force-push:

git push -f

If this seems all too complicated, you can push or force-push each new commit, and we will squash them ourselves if needed, before merging.

docs.title: Style Guidelines
docs.text:
This package follows the Google Python Style Guide with two notable exceptions:

  1. It always adds spaces around "=". This not only violates the Google guide, it violates PEP8, the foundational Python style guide from which all other resources are derived. I defy this strong, long-standing norm because I find it more readable. My brain and eyes have trouble seeing two separate objects when an equal sign is in the middle. I imagine that I am not alone in this accessibility issue. Further, as PEP8 itself notes, required spaces around equal signs are becoming increasing common with type annotations becoming part of best practices (and, as a result, signatures to classes, functions, and methods regularly include spaces around the equal signs). I realize that this will seem alien to many coders, but it is far easier on my eyes.
  2. I use some so-called "power features", primarily dunder methods, to make my interfaces easier to access and use. This is disfavored in the Google Python Style Guide because such code is often more difficult for others to read. To address that concern, I try to document and comment as to what the code is doing whenever I used any of the "power features" of Python.

Because of the first exception, the project does not use a code formatter (such as ruff format), which would remove those spaces.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text: Short answers to common questions. Each assumes import crimepy and from crimepy import analyze. Tables are amos datasets: their data is the pandas data frame.

docs.title: Load many years without running out of memory
docs.text:
Load only the states and columns you need. Both are applied while the files are read:

victims = crimepy.nibrs.load(
    'victims', '2010-2023', states = ['OH', 'MI'],
    columns = ['data_year', 'state_code', 'ori', 'incident_number',
               'victim_age_code', 'victim_sex', 'offense_1'])

docs.title: Count homicides by year and state
docs.text:
offenses = crimepy.nibrs.load('offenses', '2019-2023', columns = [
    'data_year', 'state_code', 'ori', 'incident_number', 'offense_code'])
homicides = offenses.data[offenses.data['offense_code'] == 'Murder and Nonnegligent Manslaughter']
analyze.count(homicides, ['data_year', 'state']).data

docs.title: Find hate crimes
docs.text:
offenses = crimepy.nibrs.load('offenses', 2023).data
biased = offenses[~offenses['bias_motivation_1'].isin(['None (No Bias)', 'Unknown'])]
biased['bias_motivation_1'].value_counts().head(10)

docs.title: Compare clearance rates by type of agency
docs.text:
incidents = crimepy.nibrs.tables.build('incidents', 2023, states = 'TX')
analyze.clearance_rates(incidents, by = 'agency_population_group')

docs.title: Measure time to arrest
docs.text:
arrestees = crimepy.nibrs.tables.build('arrestees', 2023, states = 'VA').data
arrestees.groupby('arrest_offense_category', observed = True)['days_to_arrest'].median()

docs.title: Use drug seizures
docs.text:
properties = crimepy.nibrs.load('properties', 2023, states = 'KY').data
seized = properties[properties['loss_type'] == 'Seized']
seized.groupby(['drug_type_1', 'drug_measure_1'], observed = True)['drug_quantity_1'].sum()

docs.title: Restrict to agencies that reported all year
docs.text:
agencies = crimepy.nibrs.load('agencies', 2023).data
full = agencies.loc[agencies['months_active'] == 12, ['data_year', 'ori']]
incidents = crimepy.nibrs.tables.build('incidents', 2023).data
incidents = incidents.merge(
    full, left_on = ['data_year', 'agency_ori'], right_on = ['data_year', 'ori'],
    suffixes = ('', '_agency'))

docs.title: Keep the codes
docs.text:
offenses = crimepy.nibrs.load('offenses', 2023, decode = False).data
offenses['offense_code'].value_counts().head()
crimepy.nibrs.codes.CODEBOOKS['offenses']['13B']

docs.title: Stack tables from different sources
docs.text:
crimepy.combine.stack keeps categories that pandas.concat would turn into plain objects:

early = crimepy.nibrs.load('victims', 2012, states = 'MI')
late = crimepy.nibrs.load('victims', 2022, states = 'MI')
both = crimepy.combine.stack([early, late])

docs.title: Read a master file you already have
docs.text:
datasets = crimepy.nibrs.read('nibrs-2016.zip', ['offenses', 'victims'], states = 'SC')
datasets['victims'].data.head()

To convert it into the data folder instead, copy it to "nibrs/raw/nibrs-2016.zip" in the data folder (such as "data/crime/nibrs/raw/nibrs-2016.zip") and run crimepy.nibrs.convert(2016).

docs.title: Model counts with amos
docs.text:
incidents = crimepy.nibrs.tables.build('incidents', '2021-2023', states = 'DE')
counts = analyze.count(
    incidents, ['agency_population_group', 'incident_month', 'incident_weekday'])
project = crimepy.Project.create({
    'general': {'seed': 43, 'label': 'count'},
    'counts_project': {'counts_workers': ['analyst', 'critic']},
    'analyst': {
        'design': 'experiment', 'criterion': 'rmse',
        'steps': ['split', 'encode', 'model'],
        'split_techniques': ['train_test'],
        'encode_techniques': ['one_hot'],
        'model_techniques': ['random_forest']},
    'critic': {'techniques': ['scorecard']}},
    item = counts)
project.scorecard.table

count returns a dataset whose label is the counts, so it is ready to model. Models cannot use dates or text, so count by numbers and categories (such as incident_month) rather than by freq, or encode the periods first.

docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text: This tutorial takes one state's NIBRS data from download to figures. It uses Delaware, whose agencies all report to NIBRS, and the years 2021 to 2023.

docs.title: Install crimepy
docs.text: pip install crimepy

docs.title: Download and convert the data
docs.text:
crimepy.nibrs.load downloads and converts any year that has not been converted, so you can start loading right away. To do it ahead of time (for example, overnight for many years), use convert:

import crimepy

crimepy.nibrs.available_years()
crimepy.nibrs.convert('2021-2023')

Each recent year is about 600 MB to download and takes a few minutes to convert. The downloads and tables are saved in the data folder (see where the data are saved), so this only happens once.

docs.title: Load a table
docs.text:
offenses = crimepy.nibrs.load('offenses', '2021-2023', states = 'DE')
offenses.data.shape
offenses.data['offense_code'].value_counts().head(10)

load returns an amos.Dataset. Its data is the table, a pandas data frame, and as you analyze and draw it, it keeps the tables and figures you make (in its tables and figures), so it is the record of your work. Each row is one offense of one incident. Codes are labels, so offense_code says "Simple Assault" rather than "13B". Load the codes instead with decode = False.

To see what a table has, look at its columns, or at its layout:

from crimepy.nibrs import layouts

[(f.name, f.kind, f.codes) for f in layouts.LAYOUTS['02']]

docs.title: Build tables for analysis
docs.text:
The segments of an incident are separate tables. tables.build joins them:

incidents = crimepy.nibrs.tables.build('incidents', '2021-2023', states = 'DE')
victims = crimepy.nibrs.tables.build('victims', '2021-2023', states = 'DE')

Each is a dataset too. incidents has one row for each incident, with its agency, the number of its offenses, victims, offenders, and arrestees, whether it had an offense of each category (such as has_assault_offenses), whether a firearm was used, whether and when someone was arrested, and whether it was cleared.

victims has one row for each victim, with its incident and agency, and the age, sex, race, and ethnicity of the first offender the victim is related to, with the relationship.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
How many incidents were there each month, and how many were cleared?

from crimepy import analyze

monthly = analyze.trend(incidents, freq = 'MS')
analyze.percent_change(monthly, periods = 12).tail()
analyze.clearance_rates(incidents, by = 'data_year')
incidents.tables['clearance_rates']

Each function returns its table, and keeps it in the dataset's tables under the name of its amos technique.

What was the rate of crime, counting only agencies that reported every month?

agencies = crimepy.nibrs.load('agencies', '2021-2023', states = 'DE')
analyze.coverage(agencies)
analyze.crime_rates(incidents, agencies, by = ['data_year', 'state'])

How were victims of aggravated assault related to their offenders?

assaults = victims.data[victims.data['offense_1'] == 'Aggravated Assault']
analyze.crosstab(assaults, 'relationship', 'victim_sex', normalize = 'columns')

docs.title: Plot
docs.text:
figure = crimepy.plot.trend(offenses, by = 'offense_category', top = 5, freq = 'QS')
figure.savefig('offenses.png')

crimepy.plot.time_heatmap(incidents).savefig('hours.png')
crimepy.plot.age_pyramid(victims, person = 'victim').savefig('victims.png')
crimepy.plot.top_values(offenses, 'location', limit = 8).savefig('places.png')
offenses.figures

Each figure is returned, and kept in the dataset's figures.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
Because the tables are amos datasets, any amos technique works on them. To model whether an incident was cleared, keep the features you want, give the dataset a label, split it, fit a model, and score it:

import amos
from amos import metrics, models, splitters

columns = ['cleared', 'firearm', 'offender_count', 'victim_count', 'arrestee_count']
features = incidents.data[columns].dropna().astype(int)
model_data = amos.Dataset.create(features, label = 'cleared', seed = 43)
splitters.Stratified().apply(model_data)
models.GradientBoosting().apply(model_data)
metrics.RocAuc().apply(model_data)
model_data.metrics['roc_auc']

(arrestee_count all but decides cleared, so the score is high: a real model of clearance would leave it out.)

docs.title: Save a table
docs.text:
A dataset's data is an ordinary pandas data frame:

victims.data.to_parquet('delaware_victims.parquet')
victims.data.to_csv('delaware_victims.csv', index = False)

Or, from the command line:

crimepy nibrs export victims 2021-2023 --states DE --output delaware_victims.csv

docs.title: Index
docs.text:
Accessible tools for crime data.

crimepy downloads, combines, munges, analyzes, and plots crime data.

Contents

Project: an amos.Project, for a study of crime data. analyze: counts crimes and computes rates, changes, and crosstabs. combine: stacks and merges tables of crime data. nibrs: tools for the FBI's National Incident-Based Reporting System. options: default settings of crimepy. plot: figures of crime data. techniques: techniques that analyze crime data, on amos datasets. utilities: small tools that the rest of crimepy shares.

docs.title: analyze
docs.text:
Analyses of crime data that researchers often need.

Each function applies one of the amos techniques of crimepy.techniques, so the same analysis can be named in a project's settings. The functions take an amos.Dataset or a data frame with one row for each event (an incident, offense, victim, or arrest), such as those of crimepy.nibrs.load and crimepy.nibrs.tables.build:

  • count: the number of rows in each group and period, as a new dataset.
  • trend: counts over time, one column for each group.
  • rates: counts per 100,000 people (or another base).
  • crime_rates: the rate of crime in each group, using the population of the agencies that reported for the whole year.
  • clearance_rates: the share of incidents cleared in each group.
  • percent_change: the change from one period to the next.
  • crosstab: counts (or shares) of two variables against each other.
  • coverage: how many agencies reported, and how many people they serve.

Each function but count returns a table. Given a dataset, it also stores the table in the dataset's tables, under the technique's name (such as "clearance_rates").

Contents

clearance_rates: the share of incidents cleared in each group. count: the number of rows in each group and period. coverage: the agencies that reported and the people they serve. crime_rates: crimes per 100,000 people, by group. crosstab: counts or shares of two variables against each other. percent_change: the change from one period to the next. rates: counts per 100,000 people. trend: counts over time, one column for each group.

def count(
    data: amos.Dataset | pd.DataFrame,
    by: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    *,
    date: str | None = None,
    freq: str | None = None,
    weight: str | None = None,
    name: str = 'count') -> amos.Dataset:
    """Returns the number of rows in each group (and period).

    Applies `crimepy.techniques.CountCrimes` to a copy of the data, so a
    dataset that is passed keeps its rows.

    Args:
        data: one row for each event.
        by: columns to group by. Defaults to `None`, which counts all rows
            (in each period, if `freq` is set).
        date: column of dates that `freq` groups by. Defaults to `None`, in
            which case it is "incident_date" if `freq` is set.
        freq: length of each period, as a `pandas` frequency ("YS" for years,
            "QS" for quarters, "MS" for months, "W" for weeks, "D" for days).
            Defaults to `None`, which does not group by period.
        weight: column whose values are summed instead of counting rows.
            Defaults to `None`.
        name: name of the column of counts. Defaults to "count".

    Returns:
        A dataset with a column for each group (and "period") and the counts,
            which are its label. Groups with no rows are left out.

    """
    return techniques.CountCrimes().apply(
        utilities.to_dataset(utilities.to_frame(data)), label = name, by = by,
        date = date, freq = freq, weight = weight, name = name)

def coverage(

    by: Sequence[str] | str = ('data_year', 'state'),
    *,

    """Returns how many agencies reported and how many people they serve.

def percent_change(
    data: amos.Dataset | pd.DataFrame | pd.Series,
    periods: int = 1) -> pd.DataFrame | pd.Series:
    """Returns the percent change from one period to the next.

    Args:
        data: counts (or rates) in each period, in order, such as a table
            from `trend`.
        periods: the number of periods to compare across (12 compares each
            month with the same month of the year before). Defaults to 1.

    Returns:
        The change, in percent, with the index of `data`.

    """
    if isinstance(data, pd.Series):
        return data.pct_change(periods = periods, fill_method = None) * 100
    return _describe(techniques.PercentChange(), data, periods = periods)

def merge(
    left: amos.Dataset | pd.DataFrame,
    right: amos.Dataset | pd.DataFrame,
    on: Sequence[str] | str,
    *,
    how: str = 'left',
    suffixes: tuple[str, str] = ('', '_right'),
    validate: str | None = None) -> amos.Dataset:
    """Joins two tables, keeping the categories of their columns.

    Args:
        left: the first table.
        right: the second table.
        on: the columns to join on, which both tables have.
        how: "left", "right", "inner", or "outer". Defaults to "left".
        suffixes: added to the names of columns (other than `on`) that both
            tables have: the first to those of `left`, the second to those of
            `right`. Defaults to ('', '_right').
        validate: checks the kind of join, as in `pandas.merge` (such as
            "many_to_one"). Defaults to `None`, which checks nothing.

    Returns:
        A dataset of the joined table.

    """
    keys = [on] if isinstance(on, str) else list(on)
    restore = {}
    items = [left, right]
    left = utilities.to_frame(left).copy()
    right = utilities.to_frame(right).copy()
    for key in keys:
        kinds = (left[key].dtype, right[key].dtype)
        if any(isinstance(k, pd.CategoricalDtype) for k in kinds):
            restore[key] = True
            left[key] = left[key].astype('object')
            right[key] = right[key].astype('object')
    joined = left.merge(
        right, on = keys,
        how = how, suffixes = suffixes,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
        validate = validate)  # type: ignore[arg-type]
    for key in restore:
        joined[key] = joined[key].astype('category')
    return _dataset(joined, items)

def stack(
    tables: Iterable[amos.Dataset | pd.DataFrame],
    *,
    source: str | None = None,
    labels: Sequence[Any] | None = None) -> amos.Dataset:
    """Stacks tables on top of each other, keeping their categories.

    Columns that are in some tables but not others are missing (`NA`) in the
    rows of the others. A column of categories in every table that has it
    stays a column of categories, with all of their categories.

    Args:
        tables: the tables to stack (such as one table for each year).
        source: name of a column to add that says which table each row came
            from. Defaults to `None`, which adds no column.
        labels: what `source` says for each table. Defaults to `None`, in
            which case the tables are numbered from 0.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if there are no tables, or `labels` does not have one
            label for each table.

    Returns:
        A dataset of the stacked table, with a new index.

    """
    items = list(tables)
    frames = [utilities.to_frame(t) for t in items]
    if not frames:
        message = 'there are no tables to stack'
        raise ValueError(message)
    if labels is not None and len(labels) != len(frames):
        message = 'labels must have one label for each table'
        raise ValueError(message)
    if source is not None:
        names = list(labels) if labels is not None else list(range(len(frames)))
        frames = [
            f.assign(**{source: name})
            for f, name in zip(frames, names, strict = True)]
    columns = list(dict.fromkeys(c for f in frames for c in f.columns))
    categorical = [
        c for c in columns
        if all(
            isinstance(f[c].dtype, pd.CategoricalDtype)
            for f in frames if c in f.columns)]
    for column in categorical:
        union = union_categoricals(
            [f[column].array for f in frames if column in f.columns],
            ignore_order = True)
        frames = [
            f.assign(**{column: f[column].cat.set_categories(union.categories)})
            if column in f.columns else f
            for f in frames]
    stacked = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index = True)
    for column in categorical:
        if not isinstance(stacked[column].dtype, pd.CategoricalDtype):
            stacked[column] = stacked[column].astype('category')
    return _dataset(stacked, items)

Figures of crime data.

Each figure is an amos.Plot, so it can be named in the "artist" stage of an amos project's settings, and it has amos's style for scientific figures (with colors that people with color blindness can tell apart). Each also has a function that draws it from an amos.Dataset (or a data frame) and returns the matplotlib figure. A dataset also keeps the figure in its figures, under the plot's name (such as "trend_plot"):

import crimepy

incidents = crimepy.nibrs.tables.build('incidents', '2021-2023', states = 'DE')
figure = crimepy.plot.trend(incidents, by = 'offense_category', top = 5)
figure.savefig('trend.png')
incidents.figures['trend_plot']

Every function takes the parameters of amos.Plot.apply: "width" and "height" (in inches), "title", "style", and "colors".

Contents

AgePyramid: ages of people by sex, as a pyramid. TimeHeatmap: events by hour of the day and day of the week. TopValues: the most common values of a column, as bars. TrendPlot: counts over time, as lines. age_pyramid: draws an AgePyramid. time_heatmap: draws a TimeHeatmap. top_values: draws a TopValues. trend: draws a TrendPlot.

def draw(
    self,
    item: amos.Dataset,
    figure: Any,
    person: str = 'victim',
    width_of_bins: int = 5,
    **kwargs: Any) -> None:
    """Draws the pyramid.

    Args:
        item: the dataset.
        figure: the figure to draw on.
        person: "victim", "offender", or "arrestee". Defaults to
            "victim".
        width_of_bins: the number of years in each bar. Defaults to 5.
        **kwargs: not used.

    """
    data = item.data[[f'{person}_age', f'{person}_sex']].dropna()
    sexes = data[f'{person}_sex'].astype('object').replace(
        {'M': 'Male', 'F': 'Female'})
    edges = np.arange(0, 100 + width_of_bins, width_of_bins)
    axes = figure.add_subplot()
    for sex, sign in (('Male', -1), ('Female', 1)):
        ages = data.loc[sexes == sex, f'{person}_age'].astype(float)
        counts, _ = np.histogram(ages, bins = edges)
        axes.barh(
            edges[:-1], sign * counts, height = width_of_bins * 0.9,
            align = 'edge', label = sex)
    ticks = axes.get_xticks()
    axes.set_xticks(ticks, [f'{abs(t):,.0f}' for t in ticks])
    axes.set_xlabel('Count')
    axes.set_ylabel(f'Age of {person}')
    axes.legend(fontsize = 'small')

    item: amos.Dataset,
    figure: Any,
    date: str = 'incident_date',
    hour: str = 'incident_hour',
    **kwargs: Any) -> None:

        date: the column of dates. Defaults to "incident_date".
        hour: the column of hours. Defaults to "incident_hour".

    axes.set_xticks(range(0, 24, 3), [f'{h:02d}' for h in range(0, 24, 3)])
    axes.set_xlabel('Hour of the day')

docs.title: techniques
docs.text:
Techniques that analyze crime data, on amos datasets.

Each technique is added to the amos library when crimepy is imported, so it can be named in the settings of any amos worker, and each can be applied to an amos.Dataset (or a data frame) directly. A describer stores its table in the dataset's tables under its name, and a shaper replaces the dataset's rows:

  • count_crimes (an amos.Shaper) turns one row for each event into one row for each group (and period), with the number of events, so that counts can be modeled (for example, with amos's poisson or negative_binomial models).
  • crime_trend (an amos.Describer) makes a table of counts over time.
  • population_rates (an amos.Describer) makes counts per 100,000 people.
  • crime_rates (an amos.Describer) makes the rate of crime in each group, using only agencies that reported all year.
  • clearance_rates (an amos.Describer) makes a table of the share of incidents cleared in each group.
  • percent_change (an amos.Describer) makes the change from one period to the next.
  • crosstab (an amos.Describer) makes counts (or shares) of two variables against each other.
  • coverage (an amos.Describer) makes a table of the agencies that reported and the people they serve, from a dataset of agencies.

The functions of crimepy.analyze apply these techniques. The figures of crimepy.plot (trend_plot, top_values, time_heatmap, and age_pyramid) are techniques too.

Contents

ClearanceRates: the share of incidents cleared in each group. CountCrimes: counts events by group and period. Coverage: the agencies that reported and the people they serve. CrimeRates: crimes per 100,000 people, by group. CrimeTrend: counts of events over time. Crosstab: counts or shares of two variables against each other. PercentChange: the change from one period to the next. PopulationRates: counts per 100,000 people.

def describe(
    self,
    item: amos.Dataset,
    by: Any = None,
    cleared: str = 'cleared',
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the share of incidents that were cleared in each group.

    Args:
        item: the dataset, with one row for each incident and a column
            saying whether it was cleared (such as from
            `crimepy.nibrs.tables.incidents`).
        by: the columns to group by. Defaults to `None`, which uses all
            rows.
        cleared: the column saying whether each incident was cleared.
            Defaults to "cleared".
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        A table with a column for each group, "incidents", "cleared", and
            "clearance_rate" (from 0 to 1).

    """
    incidents = item.data
    keys = utilities.to_names(by)
    flags = incidents[cleared].astype('boolean').fillna(False).astype(int)
    if keys:
        grouped = flags.groupby(
            [incidents[k] for k in keys], observed = True, dropna = False)
        table = grouped.agg(['size', 'sum']).reset_index()
    else:
        table = pd.DataFrame({'size': [len(flags)], 'sum': [flags.sum()]})
    table = table.rename(columns = {'size': 'incidents', 'sum': 'cleared'})
    table['clearance_rate'] = table['cleared'] / table['incidents']
    return table

def shape(
    self,
    data: pd.DataFrame,
    by: Any = None,
    date: str | None = None,
    freq: str | None = None,
    weight: str | None = None,
    name: str = 'count',
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the number of events in each group (and period).

    Args:
        data: one row for each event.
        by: the columns to group by. Defaults to `None`, which counts all
            rows (in each period, if `freq` is set).
        date: the column of dates that `freq` groups by. Defaults to
            `None`, in which case it is "incident_date" if `freq` is set.
        freq: the length of each period, as a `pandas` frequency ("YS"
            for years, "QS" for quarters, "MS" for months, "W" for weeks,
            "D" for days). Defaults to `None`, which does not group by
            period.
        weight: a column whose values are summed instead of counting
            rows. Defaults to `None`.
        name: the name of the column of counts. Defaults to "count".
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        A table with a column for each group (and "period"), and the
            counts. Groups with no rows are left out.

    """
    keys = utilities.to_names(by)
    freq = freq or None
    groupers: list[Any] = list(keys)
    if freq is not None:
        date = date or 'incident_date'
        groupers.append(pd.Grouper(key = date, freq = freq))
    if not groupers:
        total = data[weight].sum() if weight else len(data)
        return pd.DataFrame({name: [total]})
    grouped = data.groupby(groupers, observed = True, dropna = False)
    counts = grouped[weight].sum() if weight else grouped.size()
    table = counts.rename(name).reset_index()
    if freq is not None:
        table = table.rename(columns = {date: 'period'})
    return table[table[name] > 0].reset_index(drop = True)

def describe(
    self,
    item: amos.Dataset,
    by: Any = ('data_year', 'state'),
    months: Any = 12,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns how many agencies reported and how many people they serve.

    Args:
        item: a dataset of agencies, with "population" and
            "months_active".
        by: columns to group by. Defaults to ("data_year", "state").
        months: the months that an agency must have reported in to count
            as reporting for the year. Defaults to 12.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        A table with a column for each group, "agencies", "reporting"
            (the agencies that reported in at least `months` months),
            "population", "population_reporting", and "share_reporting"
            (the share of the population served by agencies that
            reported).

    """
    keys = utilities.to_names(by)
    table = item.data.copy()
    if 'covered_by_ori' in table.columns:
        table = table[table['covered_by_ori'].isna()]
    reporting = table['months_active'].fillna(0) >= int(months)
    table['_reporting'] = reporting.astype(int)
    table['_population'] = table['population'].fillna(0)
    table['_population_reporting'] = table['_population'].where(
        reporting, 0)
    summary = table.groupby(keys, observed = True).agg(
        agencies = ('ori', 'nunique'),
        reporting = ('_reporting', 'sum'),
        population = ('_population', 'sum'),
        population_reporting = (
            '_population_reporting', 'sum')).reset_index()
    share = summary['population_reporting'] / summary['population'].where(
        summary['population'] > 0)
    summary['share_reporting'] = share
    return summary

def describe(
    self,
    item: amos.Dataset,
    agencies: Any = None,
    by: Any = ('data_year', 'state'),
    months: Any = 12,
    per: float = 100_000,
    folder: Any = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the number of events per `per` people in each group.

    Args:
        item: a dataset with one row for each event (such as an
            incident), with "data_year" and "agency_ori" (or "ori").
        agencies: the agencies (a dataset or a data frame), with
            "data_year", "ori", "population", and "months_active".
            Defaults to `None`, in which case the agencies of the years
            (and states, if the data has a "state" column) of the data
            are loaded.
        by: columns of the agencies to group by. Defaults to
            ("data_year", "state").
        months: the fewest months an agency must have reported in.
            Defaults to 12.
        per: the number of people that rates are per. Defaults to
            100,000.
        folder: the data folder to load agencies from. Defaults to
            `None`, in which case it is `crimepy.utilities.data_folder()`.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        A table with a column for each group, "count", "population",
            "agencies", and "rate".

    """
    events = item.data
    if agencies is None:
        agencies = _agencies_of(events, folder)
    agencies = utilities.to_frame(agencies)
    keys = utilities.to_names(by)
    active = agencies[agencies['months_active'].fillna(0) >= int(months)]
    active = active.drop_duplicates(['data_year', 'ori'])
    key = 'agency_ori' if 'agency_ori' in events.columns else 'ori'
    columns = [k for k in keys if k not in ('data_year',)]
    joined = [c for c in columns if c in active.columns]
    kept = events[['data_year', key]].merge(
        active[['data_year', 'ori', *joined]],
        left_on = ['data_year', key], right_on = ['data_year', 'ori'],
        how = 'inner', suffixes = ('_event', ''))
    counts = kept.groupby(keys, observed = True).size().rename('count')
    people = active.groupby(keys, observed = True).agg(
        population = ('population', 'sum'), agencies = ('ori', 'nunique'))
    table = people.join(counts, how = 'left').reset_index()
    table['count'] = table['count'].fillna(0).astype('Int64')
    table = PopulationRates().describe(
        amos.Dataset(table), 'population', per = per)
    return table[[*keys, 'count', 'population', 'agencies', 'rate']]

def describe(
    self,
    item: amos.Dataset,
    by: str | None = None,
    date: str = 'incident_date',
    freq: str = 'MS',
    top: Any = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns counts over time.

    Args:
        item: the dataset, with one row for each event.
        by: the column whose values become columns. Defaults to `None`,
            which makes one column, "count".
        date: the column of dates. Defaults to "incident_date".
        freq: the length of each period, as a `pandas` frequency.
            Defaults to "MS" (months).
        top: keep only the groups with the most rows. Defaults to `None`,
            which keeps them all.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        A table indexed by the start of each period, with a column of
            counts for each group (0 in periods with none).

    """
    counted = CountCrimes().shape(item.data, by, date = date, freq = freq)
    if by is None:
        return counted.set_index('period')
    wide = counted.pivot_table(
        index = 'period', columns = by, values = 'count', aggfunc = 'sum',
        fill_value = 0, observed = True)
    if top is not None:
        largest = wide.sum().nlargest(int(top)).index
        wide = wide[largest]
    wide.columns = [str(c) for c in wide.columns]
    return wide

def describe(
    self,
    item: amos.Dataset,
    population: Any = 'population',
    on: Any = None,
    count: str = 'count',
    per: float = 100_000,
    name: str = 'rate',
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns counts per `per` people.

    Args:
        item: a dataset of counts (such as one from `count_crimes`).
        population: a column of the counts with the population, or a
            table (a dataset or a data frame) of populations to join to
            the counts on `on`, with a "population" column. Defaults to
            "population".
        on: the columns that join `population` to the counts. Defaults to
            `None`, in which case they are the columns that both have
            (other than "population").
        count: the column of counts. Defaults to "count".
        per: the number of people that rates are per. Defaults to
            100,000.
        name: name of the column of rates. Defaults to "rate".
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        The counts, with the population (if it was joined) and the rates
            (missing where the population is 0 or missing).

    """
    table = item.data.copy()
    column = 'population'
    if isinstance(population, str):
        column = population
    else:
        people = utilities.to_frame(population)
        keys = utilities.to_names(on) or [
            c for c in people.columns
            if c in table.columns and c != 'population']
        table = table.merge(people, on = keys, how = 'left')
    values = pd.to_numeric(
        table[column], errors = 'coerce').astype('Float64')
    values = values.where(values > 0)
    table[name] = table[count] / values * float(per)
    return table

def to_years(years: Any) -> list[int]:
    """Returns a sorted list of years without duplicates.

    Args:
        years: a year, a `range`, text with years separated by commas or
            spaces, a range of years as text ("2019-2023", which includes
            both ends), or an iterable of any of them.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if a year is not a whole number.

    Returns:
        The years.

    """
    found: set[int] = set()
    for item in to_list(years):
        if isinstance(item, str):
            for part in re.split(r'[,\s]+', item.strip()):
                if not part:
                    continue
                matched = _RANGE.match(part)
                if matched:
                    first, last = (int(y) for y in matched.groups())
                    found.update(range(min(first, last), max(first, last) + 1))
                else:
                    found.add(_to_year(part))
        elif isinstance(item, range):
            found.update(item)
        elif isinstance(item, Iterable):
            found.update(to_years(list(item)))
        else:
            found.add(_to_year(item))
    return sorted(found)

docs.text:
Tools for the FBI's National Incident-Based Reporting System (NIBRS).

NIBRS records each crime incident that a participating law enforcement agency reports: its offenses, the property involved, its victims, offenders, and arrestees, and arrests for less serious (Group "B") offenses. The FBI publishes a master file of every year's reports from 1991 on, which crimepy downloads, parses, and makes into flat tables, each loaded as an amos.Dataset (whose data is a pandas data frame):

  • agencies: one row for each agency (its batch header): location, population, and months reported.
  • administrative: one row for each incident: date, hour, numbers of segments, and exceptional clearance.
  • offenses: one row for each offense of an incident: offense, location, weapons, and bias motivations.
  • properties: one row for each property loss of an incident: type of loss, description, value, and drugs.
  • victims: one row for each victim: offenses, age, sex, race, injuries, and relationships to offenders.
  • offenders: one row for each offender: age, sex, race, and ethnicity.
  • arrestees: one row for each arrestee of an incident: date and type of arrest, offense, and person.
  • group_b_arrests: one row for each arrestee of a Group "B" offense.
  • window_clearances, window_properties, and window_arrestees: one row for each partial report of an incident that began before its agency reported to NIBRS.

The tables of an incident share "data_year", "ori", and "incident_number", and crimepy.nibrs.tables joins them into tables for analysis (such as one row for each victim with the incident's offenses and agency).

Contents

available_years: the years of master files that the FBI has. cde: downloads master files from the FBI's Crime Data Explorer. codes: the labels of the codes in the master files. convert: converts master files to parquet files. decode: replaces codes with their labels. download: downloads master files. layouts: where each field is in the records of the master files. load: loads a table of years as an amos.Dataset (downloading and converting them if needed). load_frame: loads a table of years as a pandas data frame. load_tables: loads several tables of years as amos datasets. munge: makes tables ready for analysis. read: reads tables straight from a master file. reader: reads and parses master files. store: converts master files to parquet files and loads them. tables: joins the tables of incidents for analysis. techniques: amos techniques for NIBRS data.

def convert(
    years: Any,
    folder: pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    *,
    tables: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    overwrite: bool = False,
    progress: bool = True,
    chunk_size: int | None = None) -> dict[int, dict[str, pathlib.Path]]:
    """Converts the NIBRS master files of years to parquet files.

    Master files that have not been downloaded are downloaded first. Tables
    that were converted before are skipped unless `overwrite` is true, and a
    year whose tables were all converted before is not read again.

    Args:
        years: a year, years, or a range of years (see
            `crimepy.utilities.to_years`).
        folder: the data folder. Defaults to `None`, in which case it is
            `crimepy.utilities.data_folder()`.
        tables: the tables to convert. Defaults to `None`, which converts
            them all.
        overwrite: whether to convert tables that were converted before (and
            to download their master files again). Defaults to `False`.
        progress: whether to show progress. Defaults to `True`.
        chunk_size: the number of records to parse at once. Defaults to
            `None`, in which case it is `crimepy.options.CHUNK_SIZE`.

    Returns:
        For each year, the path of each table's parquet file.

    """
    names = reader._wanted(tables)
    converted = {}
    for year in utilities.to_years(years):
        paths = {n: table_path(n, year, folder) for n in names}
        missing = [n for n, p in paths.items() if overwrite or not p.is_file()]
        if missing:
            master = cde.master_path(year, folder)
            if overwrite or not master.is_file():
                cde.download(
                    year, folder, overwrite = overwrite, progress = progress)
            _write(master, year, missing, paths, progress, chunk_size)
        converted[year] = paths
    return converted

def decode(
    data: _Table,
    columns: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    codebooks: Mapping[str, Mapping[str, str]] | None = None) -> _Table:
    """Replaces codes with their labels.

            every column of codes in `CODE_COLUMNS` (except age codes, which
            `add_ages` turns into years).

            `crimepy.nibrs.codes.CODEBOOKS`, by column. Defaults to `None`.

            Codes that are not in a codebook are kept.

    if isinstance(data, amos.Dataset):
        data.replace(decode(data.data, columns, codebooks))
        return data
    codebooks = codebooks or {}
    if columns is None:
        columns = [
            c for c in data.columns
            if c in CODE_COLUMNS and CODE_COLUMNS[c] not in _KEPT_CODEBOOKS]
    for column in columns:
        book = codebooks.get(column) or codes.CODEBOOKS[CODE_COLUMNS[column]]
        data[column] = _relabel(data[column], book)
    return data

def download(
    years: Any,
    folder: pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    *,
    overwrite: bool = False,
    progress: bool = True,
    timeout: float | None = None) -> list[pathlib.Path]:
    """Downloads the NIBRS master files of `years` from the CDE.

    Args:
        years: a year, years, or a range of years (see
            `crimepy.utilities.to_years`), such as 2022, [2019, 2020], or
            "2015-2023".
        folder: the data folder. Defaults to `None`, in which case it is
            `crimepy.utilities.data_folder()`.
        overwrite: whether to download a file that was downloaded before.
            Defaults to `False`.
        progress: whether to show how much of each file has been downloaded.
            Defaults to `True`.
        timeout: seconds to wait for the CDE. Defaults to `None`, in which
            case it is `crimepy.options.TIMEOUT`.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if a year has no master file.
        requests.HTTPError: if the CDE refuses a request.

    Returns:
        The paths of the zip archives, in the order of the years.

    """
    wanted = utilities.to_years(years)
    if not wanted:
        message = 'there are no years to download'
        raise ValueError(message)
    timeout = timeout or options.TIMEOUT
    first, last = _year_range(timeout)
    missing = [y for y in wanted if not first <= y <= last]
    if missing:
        message = (
            f'the CDE has NIBRS master files for {first} to {last}, so there '
            f'are none for {missing}')
        raise ValueError(message)
    paths = []
    for year in wanted:
        path = master_path(year, folder)
        if path.is_file() and not overwrite:
            logger.info(f'{path} was downloaded before')
        else:
            _fetch(_KEY.format(year = year), path, progress, timeout)
        paths.append(path)
    return paths

def load_frame(
    table: str,
    years: Any,
    *,
    folder: pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    states: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    columns: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    decode: bool = True,
    fetch: bool = True,
    progress: bool = True) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Loads a table of NIBRS data for years into a `pandas` data frame.

    The years are stacked into one table, with "data_year" saying which
    master file each row came from. `load` returns the same table as an
    `amos.Dataset`.

    Args:
        table: the name of the table: "administrative", "offenses",
            "properties", "victims", "offenders", "arrestees",
            "group_b_arrests", "window_clearances", "window_properties",
            "window_arrestees", or "agencies".
        years: a year, years, or a range of years (see
            `crimepy.utilities.to_years`).
        folder: the data folder. Defaults to `None`, in which case it is
            `crimepy.utilities.data_folder()`.
        states: postal abbreviations (such as "DE") or numeric state codes
            of the states to keep. Defaults to `None`, which keeps every
            state.
        columns: the columns to load. Defaults to `None`, which loads them
            all. Columns that `crimepy.nibrs.munge.prepare` adds (such as
            "state") are added if the columns they come from are loaded.
        decode: whether to replace codes with their labels. Defaults to
            `True`.
        fetch: whether to download and convert years that have not been
            converted. Defaults to `True`.
        progress: whether to show the progress of downloads and conversions.
            Defaults to `True`.

    Raises:
        FileNotFoundError: if a year has not been converted and `fetch` is
            false.

    Returns:
        The table.

    """
    schema = reader.schema(table)
    paths = []
    for year in utilities.to_years(years):
        path = table_path(table, year, folder)
        if not path.is_file():
            if not fetch:
                message = (
                    f'the {table} of {year} have not been converted: use '
                    f'crimepy.nibrs.convert({year}) or fetch = True')
                raise FileNotFoundError(message)
            convert(year, folder, progress = progress)
        paths.append(path)
    if not paths:
        message = 'there are no years to load'
        raise ValueError(message)
    if columns is not None:
        unknown = [c for c in columns if c not in schema.names]
        if unknown:
            message = f'{table!r} has no columns {unknown}'
            raise KeyError(message)
    dataset = ds.dataset(
        [str(p) for p in paths], schema = schema, format = 'parquet')
    kept = reader._state_codes(states)
    condition = (
        ds.field('state_code').isin([c.decode() for c in kept])
        if kept else None)
    loaded = dataset.to_table(
        columns = list(columns) if columns is not None else None,
        filter = condition)
    return munge.prepare(munge.to_pandas(loaded), table, decode = decode)

def read(
    path: pathlib.Path | str,
    names: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    *,
    year: int | None = None,
    states: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    decode: bool = True,
    chunk_size: int | None = None,
    limit: int | None = None) -> dict[str, amos.Dataset]:
    """Reads tables from a master file into `amos` datasets.

    Everything is kept in memory, so reading a whole recent year (tens of
    millions of records) needs a lot of it. To work with whole years, convert
    them to parquet files once with `crimepy.nibrs.convert` and load what you
    need with `crimepy.nibrs.load`. `read` suits a few states, a few tables,
    or a quick look (with `limit`).

    Args:
        path: path of a master file (see `open_master`).
        names: the tables to read (see `crimepy.nibrs.layouts.TABLES`).
            Defaults to `None`, which reads them all.
        year: the year of the master file. Defaults to `None`, in which case
            it is found from the file's name.
        states: postal abbreviations or numeric state codes of the states to
            keep. Defaults to `None`, which keeps every state.
        decode: whether to replace codes with their labels (see
            `crimepy.nibrs.munge.prepare`). Defaults to `True`.
        chunk_size: the number of records to parse at once. Defaults to
            `None`, in which case it is `crimepy.options.CHUNK_SIZE`.
        limit: the number of records to read before stopping. Defaults to
            `None`, which reads them all.

    Returns:
        A dataset for each table, by name, whose `data` is the table.

    """
    wanted = _wanted(names)
    parts: dict[str, list[pa.Table]] = {name: [] for name in wanted}
    for chunk in tables(
        path, wanted, year = year, states = states, chunk_size = chunk_size,
        limit = limit):
        for name, table in chunk.items():
            parts[name].append(table)
    datasets = {}
    for name, pieces in parts.items():
        table = (
            pa.concat_tables(pieces) if pieces
            else schema(name).empty_table())
        frame = munge.prepare(munge.to_pandas(table), name, decode = decode)
        datasets[name] = amos.Dataset.create(frame)
    return datasets

def download(
    years: Any,
    folder: pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    *,
    overwrite: bool = False,
    progress: bool = True,
    timeout: float | None = None) -> list[pathlib.Path]:
    """Downloads the NIBRS master files of `years` from the CDE.

    Args:
        years: a year, years, or a range of years (see
            `crimepy.utilities.to_years`), such as 2022, [2019, 2020], or
            "2015-2023".
        folder: the data folder. Defaults to `None`, in which case it is
            `crimepy.utilities.data_folder()`.
        overwrite: whether to download a file that was downloaded before.
            Defaults to `False`.
        progress: whether to show how much of each file has been downloaded.
            Defaults to `True`.
        timeout: seconds to wait for the CDE. Defaults to `None`, in which
            case it is `crimepy.options.TIMEOUT`.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if a year has no master file.
        requests.HTTPError: if the CDE refuses a request.

    Returns:
        The paths of the zip archives, in the order of the years.

    """
    wanted = utilities.to_years(years)
    if not wanted:
        message = 'there are no years to download'
        raise ValueError(message)
    timeout = timeout or options.TIMEOUT
    first, last = _year_range(timeout)
    missing = [y for y in wanted if not first <= y <= last]
    if missing:
        message = (
            f'the CDE has NIBRS master files for {first} to {last}, so there '
            f'are none for {missing}')
        raise ValueError(message)
    paths = []
    for year in wanted:
        path = master_path(year, folder)
        if path.is_file() and not overwrite:
            logger.info(f'{path} was downloaded before')
        else:
            _fetch(_KEY.format(year = year), path, progress, timeout)
        paths.append(path)
    return paths
